1268.tomorrow: hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna
1268.howItsDone: In Vedic ritual, offerings are poured into a sacred fire while hymns to Agni are recited; at home, some Hindu households light a lamp at dawn or dusk, and some keep a fire offering, homa, on special days.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SIXTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday closed a week on the Gayatri in context, ending with Krishna in the Gita: among meters, I am the Gayatri.
screen: `ONE VERSE, SEEN FROM SIX SIDES.`

segments.voice: Click, click, whoomp. A blue ring of flame on a gas stove. A match struck for a birthday candle. A lamp lit in a window. Fire is easy to use all day without a second thought. The Rig Veda opens with a hymn to that fire, and it doesn't treat it as a tool. It treats it as someone. For four days, four of the Veda's voices: Agni, Indra, Ushas and Varuna. Today: Agni, the fire.
screen: `CLICK, CLICK, WHOOMP.` → `NOT A TOOL. SOMEONE.` → `FOUR VOICES. TODAY, AGNI.`

segments.voice: Agni is the Sanskrit word for fire, and in the Vedas he's also the god in the fire. The hymn that opens the Rig Veda, book one, hymn one, begins agnim ile purohitam: I praise Agni, the one placed in front. He's called a priest, the one who calls the gods and carries the offering: when something is poured into the sacred fire, the hymn says, Agni takes it to the gods. So fire stands in the middle, on the ground, in the house, and reaching toward heaven. That's the familiar part. Two later verses bring it closer. One says, in paraphrase: to you, Agni, day after day, we come with our thoughts, bringing homage. Not on festival days only. Every day. Some translators also hear in that verse the edges of the day, dusk and dawn, the hours the Gayatri is kept. Then the hymn's last verse, a warm one: sa nah piteva sunave, agne supayano bhava. Be easy to approach for us, Agni, as a father is to his son. Stay with us, for our good. The great power that carries offerings to the gods is asked to be approachable: not distant, not dangerous, not grand, but like a father a child can walk right up to. That's how the hymnbook begins. Not with thunder, but with a fire in the house, asked to be near.
screen: `AGNI: FIRE, AND THE GOD IN IT.` · `THE PRIEST WHO CARRIES THE OFFERING.` · `DAY AFTER DAY, WITH HOMAGE.` · `EASY TO REACH, AS A FATHER TO A SON.`

segments.voice: If you have a candle or lamp and it's safe, light it and set it a little in front of you; if not, bring to mind a flame you know well, a stove, a diya, a birthday candle. Let your eyes rest on it without staring, noticing how it leans, flickers and steadies again, and when attention drifts, come back to the flame. If you pray, hold the hymn's last line: be easy to approach, as a father to his son.
Hymns to Agni. Agni is fire, and the god in the fire, the priest who carries the offering, asked in the Rig Veda's opening hymn to be easy to approach, like a father to his son. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna. The fire comes first, and close. See you tomorrow.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hymns to Agni: the fire in the house, asked to be easy to approach, as a father to his son.

segments.voice: "Where is he?" people ask. "He isn't real," others answer. It could be an argument at a dinner table this week. It's a line from a hymn in the Rig Veda, book two, and the god being doubted is Indra: the storm, the warrior, the one who breaks the dam and lets the rivers run. The hymn could have left the doubters out. Instead it quotes them, right in the middle of the praise. Today: the second voice, Indra.
screen: `"WHERE IS HE?"` → `"HE ISN'T REAL."` → `A HYMN THAT QUOTES ITS DOUBTERS.`

segments.voice: Indra is the mighty one of the Rig Veda's storms. In its stories he fights Vritra, a serpent coiled around the waters, holding them back, and when Indra strikes him down, the rivers pour free. He drinks soma, rides with the storm, and stands with those who call on him. Book two, hymn twelve, praises him in a shape you can hear even in paraphrase. Verse after verse tells something he did: he steadied the shaking earth, spread out the sky, killed the serpent and set the rivers flowing. And verse after verse ends the same way. Sa janasa indrah. He, O people, is Indra. Then, in the fifth verse, the hymn turns. In paraphrase: the terrible one, about whom they ask, where is he? About whom they say, he is not. The singer's answer isn't an argument. It's an invitation: put your trust in him. He, O people, is Indra. A hymn of praise names, out loud, the people who don't believe in the god it praises. It doesn't hide the question or pretend nobody asks it. It lets the question stand, answers it with trust, and goes on singing. Earlier on this path the Nasadiya Sukta asked who really knows how the world began. Here, a hymn to the god of the storm makes room for someone saying he isn't there at all.
screen: `INDRA FREES THE WATERS.` · `"HE, O PEOPLE, IS INDRA."` · `"WHERE IS HE?" "HE IS NOT."` · `THE QUESTION STAYS IN THE HYMN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you're unsure of, about life, faith, a person or yourself, and let it be asked without arguing or settling it. Beside it, find one thing you do trust, even something small: the floor holding you, the breath coming back, someone who has shown up for you. Hold both, and if you pray, offer both.
Hymns to Agni, and today, to Indra. In Rig Veda book two, hymn twelve, each verse ends, he, O people, is Indra, and one verse quotes those who say, he is not. Today's word.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna reached Indra, in a hymn that quotes its doubters, where is he, he is not, and answers with trust.

segments.voice: The window is black. Then, without any moment you could point to, it's gray. Then a thin band low in the sky turns the color of a peach. A bird starts. A car door shuts somewhere. A neighbor's light comes on. Everything is getting ready. In the Rig Veda, this in-between light has a name: Ushas, the dawn, and she is a goddess. Today: the third voice.
screen: `BLACK, THEN GRAY, THEN PEACH.` → `EVERYTHING GETS READY.` → `USHAS, THE DAWN.`

segments.voice: In the Rig Veda Ushas is pictured as a young woman in bright clothes, showing her brightness in the east. One hymn to her, book one, hymn one hundred thirteen, watches what she does. In paraphrase: she wakes every living thing. She sends one person off to power, another to worship, another to seek a goal. The sleeper stirs; the one lying down gets up. The world that was still starts moving because she has come. Then the hymn looks at time. She follows the path of the dawns gone before, it says, and she's the first of all the endless dawns still to come. Every morning stands in a line: behind it, every dawn there has been; ahead, every dawn there will be. Then a quieter verse. In paraphrase: those mortals who saw the earlier dawns have gone. Now she is seen by us. And those who will see her in days to come are on their way. It's a hymn about morning that doesn't look away from time passing. The people who watched dawn before are gone, and others will watch after. The verse doesn't dwell on fear. Some readers hear company in it instead: the same dawn, seen by those before, by us now, and by those still coming.
screen: `USHAS: DAWN, AND A GODDESS.` · `SHE WAKES WHAT IS LIVING.` · `FIRST OF THE DAWNS STILL TO COME.` · `THEY SAW HER; WE SEE HER; OTHERS WILL.`

segments.voice: Face a window or any light, close your eyes for a few breaths, then open them slowly and notice the first thing you see clearly. With your eyes half open, bring to mind someone who saw many mornings before you, a grandparent or a teacher, and someone who'll see mornings after, and let them sit with you, one on each side. If you pray, offer the morning to them both.
Hymns to Agni, and today, to Ushas. The dawn goddess who wakes every living thing, the first of the dawns to come, seen by those before us and by those after. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna. Each morning joins a long line of mornings. Until tomorrow.

segments.voice: A friend stops answering. No fight, no reason given. The messages just go unread. So the scrolling starts: back through the thread, looking for the line that went wrong. Then the asking around: did they say anything to you? A hymn in the Rig Veda, book seven, follows almost exactly those steps. Only the one who has gone quiet is Varuna, the god who keeps the order of the world. Today: the fourth voice.
screen: `A FRIEND GOES QUIET.` → `SCROLLING BACK FOR THE WRONG LINE.` → `THE ONE GONE QUIET IS VARUNA.`

segments.voice: In the Rig Veda Varuna keeps rita, the order that holds the world together: the sun on its path, the rivers in their beds, truth between people. He sees what's done in secret. Tradition gives book seven to the family of the sage Vasishtha, and hymn eighty-six there is a singer's plea to Varuna. It opens in wonder at his greatness, then turns personal. In paraphrase: when will I be close to Varuna again? Will he accept my offering without anger? The singer goes looking for the cause. I ask, wanting to know my wrong, he says; I go to the wise. And the wise all give the same answer: Varuna is angry with you. So he asks Varuna directly. What was my great offense, that you would strike down your friend, the one who praises you? Tell me, so I can come to you, free of it. Then he asks to be released from what his fathers did and from what he has done himself, as a calf is untied from its rope. And he names the causes plainly: it wasn't my own will. It was drink, anger, dice, thoughtlessness. Some readers hear an excuse there; others, an honest naming of what pulls a person off course. Either way, the hymn doesn't wallow. It asks, listens, names what went wrong, and asks to be untied: not a stranger begging, but a friend asking to be close again.
screen: `VARUNA, WHO KEEPS THE ORDER.` · `"WHAT WAS MY WRONG?"` · `UNTIED, LIKE A CALF FROM A ROPE.` · `DRINK, ANGER, DICE, THOUGHTLESSNESS.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna reached the fourth voice: a singer asking Varuna what he had done wrong. Fire, storm, dawn, order.
screen: `FIRE, STORM, DAWN, ORDER.`

segments.voice: A wedding invitation arrives. Heavy card, gold edges, and in the middle two names joined by an ampersand: Priya and Daniel. Not one name, and the other somewhere below. One line, one symbol, because the invitation is about the two of them together. Some old hymns work the same way. In the Rig Veda a god is often praised alone, Agni in one hymn, Indra in the next. But some hymns call two gods at once, and Sanskrit can join their names into one word, so the pair is addressed like a single guest. Today: the gods who come in pairs.
screen: `TWO NAMES, ONE AMPERSAND.` → `SOME HYMNS CALL TWO GODS AT ONCE.` → `THE GODS WHO COME IN PAIRS.`

segments.voice: Sanskrit grammar doesn't stop at one and many. It keeps a form just for a pair, and it lets two names fuse. Mitra and Varuna become Mitravaruna, one word, spoken in the form for two. Indra and Agni become Indragni. Neither name is lost; they're just said together. The Rig Veda has hymns to both pairs. Varuna you've met as the keeper of order. Mitra, as an everyday word, means friend, and in the hymns he stands beside Varuna. So the keeper of order isn't praised alone. He's praised next to a friend: the order that holds the world, and friendship, named in one breath. Indra and Agni make a different pair: the storm that breaks the drought, and the fire on the household hearth. A hymn can ask them to come together to the same offering, as if the two strengths need each other. And Ushas, the dawn, keeps company with Agni without any grammar at all. The fire is lit at daybreak, so in the hymns the two arrive together, the light in the sky and the flame on the ground. The poets didn't only picture each god on a pedestal of their own. They also pictured them as companions, called in twos, sharing a seat. Look at almost anything good you did this week, and there's an ampersand in it somewhere.
screen: `A GRAMMAR FOR TWO.` · `MITRA AND VARUNA: FRIEND AND ORDER.` · `INDRA AND AGNI: STORM AND HEARTH.` · `USHAS AND AGNI ARRIVE AT DAWN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind two people who are better together than apart, a couple, two friends, a parent and child, and hold their names side by side, joined like Mitravaruna, noticing what each brings that the other doesn't. Then ask who you're paired with, and rest with the name that comes. If you pray, hold that pair in prayer.
Hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna. Today, the paired hymns: Mitra and Varuna, Indra and Agni, fused into one word and praised together. Today's word.

1273.title: hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna
1273.hook: "take care." "love, Mom." a sign-off said over and over can still mean everything. hymns in the Rig Veda's seventh book share one
1273.carry: hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna
1273.howItsDone: Hymns in the seventh book of the Rig Veda, credited to the family of the seer Vasishtha, close with the refrain yuyam pata svastibhih sada nah, and Vedic chanters learn it with the hymns.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna, called in pairs: Mitra and Varuna, Indra and Agni, joined in one word.
screen: `THE GODS WHO COME IN PAIRS.`

segments.voice: Take care. Drive safe. Love, Mom. Text me when you get home. Some goodbyes get said so often they're worn smooth, like a step everyone uses. And still, if the person who always says drive safe forgets one day, it's noticed. A sign-off that sounds routine can carry a whole relationship. The Rig Veda has one. In its seventh book, the hymns credited to the seer Vasishtha's family, one closing line returns at the end of hymn after hymn: to Agni, to Indra, to Ushas, to Varuna. Today, the last day on these hymns: how they say goodbye.
screen: `TAKE CARE. DRIVE SAFE. LOVE, MOM.` → `WORN SMOOTH, STILL MEANT.` → `HOW THE HYMNS SAY GOODBYE.`

segments.voice: The line is yuyam pata svastibhih sada nah. In plain English: you, protect us always with blessings. Svasti is well-being, things going well. Pata means protect, keep. Sada, always. Nah, us. Now listen to the first word. Yuyam is you, but plural: you all. Even when a hymn has spent its whole length praising one god, the dawn, say, or the fire, the last line can turn and speak to the gods together. Thank you, Agni, for this morning, and all of you: keep us well. The hymn to Varuna from two days ago, where the singer asks what he did wrong, closes this way too. After all that worry, the ending is the same steady line as the hymns of praise. Whatever happened in the middle, the sign-off doesn't change. A refrain isn't lazy writing. It's a promise of return. The singer says it at the end of the dawn hymn and again at the end of the fire hymn, and the repeating is part of the meaning: keep us well, always, the way we keep coming back. And notice what's asked for. Not victory, not riches. Just svasti, well-being, kept. Each of the four voices has had its day. This is how their hymns close: one ordinary, enormous wish, said to all of them at once.
screen: `YUYAM PATA SVASTIBHIH SADA NAH.` · `YUYAM: YOU, PLURAL. ALL OF YOU.` · `THE SAME LINE, AFTER PRAISE OR WORRY.` · `SVASTI: WELL-BEING, KEPT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people you'll see or talk to today, one face at a time, and with each out-breath wish them one plain thing: be well. Then widen it the way yuyam does, to all of them together, the people they love, and the ones you won't meet. If you pray, pray for them in your own words.
Hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna. Today, the closing line of hymns in the seventh book: you all, protect us always with well-being. Today's word.

1274.title: the Sama Veda as song
1274.hook: a poem on a page and the same poem sung are not the same thing. the Sama Veda takes hymn verses and gives them a tune
1274.howItsDone: The Sama Veda is learned from a teacher by ear, melody and all, and in the Vedic rites its chants belong to the priests who sing.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna said goodbye: you all, protect us always with well-being.
screen: `KEEP US WELL, ALWAYS.`

segments.voice: Read a song lyric off a screen, flat, with no tune. Something's missing. Every word is there, and yet the line just sits on the page. Now hear it sung. It stretches where it wants to. A short word holds for three beats; a syllable climbs and falls. Nothing about the words changed, and everything about them did. This week we've read the Rig Veda's hymns as words. Hindu tradition keeps another Veda that does to verses like these what a melody does to a lyric. Today: the Sama Veda, the Veda as song.
screen: `A LYRIC READ FLAT.` → `THE SAME LINE, SUNG.` → `THE VEDA AS SONG.`

segments.voice: The word saman means a chant, a melody, and the Sama Veda is the Veda of those melodies. Here's the surprise: it doesn't bring a new set of words. Its verses are ones that also appear in the Rig Veda, from hymns like the ones we've heard all week, gathered and set to tune. It isn't a second set of lyrics. It's the music. Listen to where it begins. Its opening verse is a call to the fire: agna a yahi vitaye. Come, Agni, to the feast. The same Agni whose hymns opened the Rig Veda opens the songbook too, and here the invitation is sung. Why keep a whole Veda of melody? Because in the old rites different priests had different jobs. Some recited the verses. Some sang them. The Sama Veda belongs to the singers. Their task wasn't to say what the hymn means, but to carry it on a voice that rises, holds and falls, so the words don't just land. They ring. Tradition treats the melody itself as sacred, not decoration added later, and the chants were handed on from teacher to student by ear. Say good morning to someone flatly, then as if you're glad they're here. Same two words. The tune is part of what you said.
screen: `SAMAN: A CHANT, A MELODY.` · `RIG VEDA VERSES, SET TO TUNE.` · `IT OPENS: COME, AGNI, TO THE FEAST.` · `THE TUNE IS PART OF WHAT IS SAID.`

segments.voice: Breathe in through the nose, and on the out-breath hum one quiet, low, steady note for as long as the breath lasts, feeling where it buzzes: lips, nose, chest. Don't make a tune; just let the voice ride the breath out, or, if humming isn't possible where you are, hum without sound and feel the breath alone. If you pray, let one hum be your prayer.
The Sama Veda as song. Saman, melody: verses from the Rig Veda's hymns, set to tune and sung. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: the Sama Veda as song. Same words, and now they ring. Until tomorrow.
